text:
# Pārājika Pāḷi - First Pārājika

17. Or furthermore, if a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the <term>sikkhāpada</term> <gloss>training rules</gloss> feels ashamed, loathes them, and desires the state of a householder <note>meaning he wishes to return to lay life</note>... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "I have a mother, she will support me," and thus he gives up the training. Or he says and declares: "I have a father, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a brother, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a sister, she will support me." He says and declares: "I have a son, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a daughter, he will support me." He says and declares: "I have a wife, she will support me." He says and declares: "I have relatives, they will support me." He says and declares: "I have friends, they will support me." He says and declares: "I have a village, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have a town, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have a field, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have property, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have gold, I will live by means of that." He says and declares: "I have bullion <note>original: hiraññaṃ; specifically uncoined gold or wealth</note>, I will live by means of that." ... He says and declares: "I have a craft <note>original: sippaṃ; a trade or skill</note>, I will live by means of that." In this way, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

18. Or furthermore, if a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the training rule feels ashamed, loathes it, and desires the state of a householder ... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "It is difficult to do." He says and declares: "It is hard to perform." He says and declares: "It is difficult to maintain." He says and declares: "It is not easy to maintain." He says and declares: "I am not able." He says and declares: "I do not wish to." He says and declares: "I do not find delight." ... He says and declares: "I am not satisfied." In this way too, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

19. And how, monks, is there an opening of weakness and the training is renounced? Here, monks, a monk is dissatisfied, bored, wanting to leave, and while speaking of the training rule feels ashamed, loathes it, and desires the state of a householder ... through various ways of expressing inability, he says and declares: "I renounce the Buddha." In this way too, monks, there is an opening of weakness and the training is renounced.

<summary>This page details the specific verbal declarations a monk might make to renounce his training, including citing family support, material wealth, or personal inability to endure the monastic life. It establishes the legalistic framework for how a monk formally leaves the order by expressing a preference for lay life or a rejection of the Triple Gem.</summary>

<keywords>renunciation of training, monastic rules, Vinaya, lay life, family support, personal inability, Buddha, Parajika</keywords>
